flashcards.q: Name three valid stop conditions for an agent loop, and why you need at least two simultaneously.
flashcards.a: Max-iteration cap, model-emitted 'done' signal, cost/token budget ceiling. Need 2+ because relying solely on the model to say 'I'm done' fails when the model gets stuck reasoning in circles.

flashcards.q: Why does dense-vector-only retrieval fail on exact-match queries, and what fixes it?
flashcards.a: An embedding model can rate a semantically similar but lexically wrong result higher than an exact but less 'fluent' match -- fails on SKUs, error codes, proper nouns, acronyms. Fix: hybrid search, fusing BM25 (lexical) with dense vectors, typically via Reciprocal Rank Fusion: score = sum(1/(k+rank_i)), k~60.

flashcards.q: What do HNSW's M and ef_search parameters each control, and which is the cheaper tuning lever?
flashcards.a: M = max links per node per layer (recall vs. memory/build-time, requires reindex to change). ef_search = query-time candidate list size (recall vs. latency, cheapest lever, no reindex needed). Recall@k is a tunable curve, not a fixed property of 'using HNSW.'

flashcards.q: Recall@10 is 85%, product wants 95%. What are your levers in order of cost?
flashcards.a: 1) Raise ef_search (cheapest, query-time only). 2) Raise M (requires full reindex, more memory). 3) Check if the embedding model itself is the ceiling -- compare ANN recall against brute-force exact search on the same query set; if exact search also fails, the embedding is the problem, not the index.

flashcards.q: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder: what's the architectural difference, and why can't a cross-encoder replace retrieval entirely?
flashcards.a: Bi-encoder embeds query and doc independently (index-able, cheap, but no query-doc attention). Cross-encoder concatenates query+doc and runs jointly through a transformer (catches token-level interactions, but nothing to precompute -- score depends on the query, unknown until query time). Can't scale to a full corpus per query, so it only reranks a small top-k.

flashcards.q: Give a measurable definition of hallucination, and the two-tier eval pipeline that catches a regression.
flashcards.a: A claim in the output not supported by the retrieved context/source, stated with unwarranted confidence. Pipeline: fast tolerance-based check gating every deploy (aggregate groundedness score against a golden set of real production queries) + slower thorough check (human review or LLM-judge ensemble) running nightly/pre-release.

flashcards.q: Name two concrete failure modes of 'just put everything in the context window' even with a 1M-token model.
flashcards.a: Lost-in-the-middle (models attend more reliably to content near the start/end than content buried mid-context) and cost/latency scaling (attention cost and time-to-first-token both grow with context length -- not free even when it fits).

flashcards.q: What's the real test for whether splitting a monolithic agent into multiple specialized agents is justified?
flashcards.a: Split only when failure modes, scaling profiles, or retry/rollback semantics genuinely differ between responsibilities. Most reported multi-agent failures are 'one agent's worth of logic with extra network hops and an ambiguous failure mode,' not genuine decomposition.

flashcards.q: What does MCP/FastMCP actually add over writing function-calling tools directly, and when should you skip it?
flashcards.a: Protocol-level decoupling: a tool surface becomes a versioned contract a second, unrelated consumer can use without importing the first app's code. Skip it for a single application with no reuse case -- in-process function calling is simpler with one fewer moving part.

flashcards.q: Where does prompt injection actually live, and what's the real architectural mitigation (not the linguistic one)?
flashcards.a: Any content the model reads that originated outside your control can contain text crafted to look like an instruction, and the model can't reliably distinguish system instructions from embedded ones -- both arrive as tokens in the same context. Real mitigation: untrusted content is data the model reasons ABOUT, never instructions it obeys; privileged/irreversible actions are gated by CODE outside the model (allowlist, human confirmation), never by a system-prompt instruction alone.

flashcards.q: Rank structured-output mitigations by reliability, and state what none of them guarantee.
flashcards.a: Constrained/grammar-based decoding (structural guarantee, strongest) > few-shot examples + strict system prompt (behavioral nudge, weak) > regex extraction + retry-on-failure (fallback, non-zero failure rate). None guarantee SEMANTIC correctness -- a syntactically valid JSON can still call the wrong tool with hallucinated arguments.

flashcards.q: Fine-tuning vs. RAG: what's each actually good for, and what's the diagnostic for which one a failure needs?
flashcards.a: Fine-tuning teaches STYLE/format/behavior; poorly suited to FACTS that change (stale the moment data changes, needs retraining). RAG serves facts that update the moment the index refreshes. Diagnostic: wrong/outdated facts -> retrieval problem; wrong tone/format/reasoning style regardless of facts given -> fine-tuning problem.

flashcards.q: Your RAG-as-tool call times out, returns zero results, or returns uniformly low-confidence results. Are these one failure mode or three?
flashcards.a: Three distinct failure modes needing distinct handlers: timeout -> bounded retry + graceful degradation with an explicit caveat; zero results -> bounded query-reformulation retry or honest 'not found,' never a fabricated fill-in; low confidence -> lower stated certainty or surface the uncertainty, never present as solid grounding. Never one generic retry-and-hope.

flashcards.q: Why is fine-tuning on domain Q&A pairs sometimes correlated with a HIGHER hallucination rate, not lower?
flashcards.a: It can teach the model the STYLE of correctness (in-domain vocabulary, plausible structure) without improving factual grounding, and can suppress the base model's calibrated uncertainty -- a model that would have hedged now speaks with unearned fine-tuned confidence.

flashcards.q: This round's calibration rule: what score band should feel harder to earn here than in the ML round, and why?
flashcards.a: HIRE (14-17/20) and above should be harder to earn, because GenAI is the student's strongest domain and a shallow pass here is a meaningful red flag for a principal-level GenAI role, not an acceptable outcome.
